explainer.heading: Background
explainer.body: An adapted excerpt from Shakespeare’s comedy, set in a fairyland in Athens. Oberon, the Fairy King, wants Titania’s boy attendant for his chores, but Titania refuses, so he puts her under a spell: on waking she becomes fond of the first face she sees. She falls for Bottom, an Athenian peasant who has been given the head of an ass (donkey).
explainer.example: Theme: dreams, magic and fantasy — comedy.

explainer.heading: Titania and Bottom
explainer.body: Titania sits Bottom on a flower-strewn bed, strokes his cheeks, puts musk roses in his hair and pets his big ears. Bottom orders the fairies around: Peaseblossom must scratch his head; Cobweb must kill a red-hipped bumblebee and bring its honey without breaking the honey sac; Mustardseed must help scratch, because his face feels hairy and he is “a very sensitive ass”.

explainer.heading: Funny requests
explainer.body: Asked about music, Bottom wants percussion. For food he wants good dry oats and a bundle of sweet hay; when offered squirrel’s nuts, he prefers dried peas. He wants to sleep, so Titania sends the fairies away and wraps him in her arms like ivy around an elm.
explainer.example: Comedy: a queen treating a donkey-headed peasant like a prince.

explainer.heading: The spell is broken
explainer.body: Oberon tells Robin (Puck) that he mocked Titania and agreed to stop only if she gave him her attendant — she did at once, so the boy is now his. He drops a flower’s nectar on her eyelid: “Diana’s flower has more power than Cupid’s.” Titania wakes and says she dreamt she loved an ass. Oberon winks at Robin: “was it really a dream?” Puck will remove the ass’s head so Bottom can return to Athens.

explainer.heading: Titania’s song
explainer.body: In a lyrical rhyming verse, Titania describes the “dream”: a man with an ass’s head; she got to know him, he told funny stories and made her happy — but wasn’t she a little mad? She is glad it was just a dream. Tone: light-hearted, amused, relieved.

explainer.heading: Vocabulary & grammar
explainer.body: Adjective suffixes -y / -ly: hair → hairy, friend → friendly, love → lovely, sleep → sleepy. Expressions with “out of”: out of the blue, out of control, out of breath, out of date. Kinds of sentences (2): imperative (command/request: “Scratch my head.”) and exclamatory (strong feeling, ends with !: “What a dream!”).

explainer.heading: Writing & author
explainer.body: A descriptive essay uses the five senses, vivid adjectives, similes and a clear order (place/time/feeling). William Shakespeare, the “Bard of Avon”, born 1564 in Stratford-upon-Avon, playwright, poet and actor. Famous works: Hamlet, The Tempest, Macbeth, King Lear.

questions.model: Peaseblossom had to scratch his head; Cobweb had to kill a red-hipped bumblebee and bring him its honey; Mustardseed had to help Peaseblossom scratch him.

questions.q: Why did Oberon decide to break the spell?
questions.model: Titania had given him her boy attendant, which was what he wanted. The spell was only to divert her attention, so once he had the boy, he released her.
points: Spell only to divert her; no longer needed

questions.q: How does the excerpt create comedy through magic and Bottom’s behaviour?
questions.model: The comedy comes from the spell: the proud Fairy Queen falls in love with Bottom, a peasant with an ass’s head. She treats him like a prince — flowers, roses in his hair, petting his ears. Bottom behaves like a donkey but orders fairies like a lord: scratch my head, bring honey, he wants percussion, oats, hay and dried peas. Oberon laughs at Titania, and when she wakes she thinks it was only a dream, while he winks at Robin. Her lyrical song about loving an ass adds to the fun.
points: Spell makes Queen love a donkey-headed peasant
Bottom’s donkey-like wants but lordly orders
Oberon’s laughter / “was it really a dream?” / Titania’s song
